messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
messages.body_plain:
I would say it's because the contamination is one-sided with presence/absence data, which causes the effect size to be underestimated on average.  With abundance, the imperfect detection is an equal opportunity phenomenon so the relative comparisons still hold.  The stark difference in accuracy/precision also highlights how hungry the logistic regression is for data, and the greater relative value of counts over 0/1s.

I bet that even if you model p, the occupancy slopes will be slightly underestimated.

messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
messages.body_plain:
I think it's because imperfect detection for presense/absence is imperfect detection of the species, which is related with abundance (the species is more detectable where it is more abundant). Because abundance is greater where occupancy is greater, imperfect detection declines with increasing abundance and increasing occupancy, resulting less of an upward correction of occupancy at the right side of the gradient. For abundance, imperfect detection is at the individual level and therefore not related with abundance and therefore even across the covariate gradient.

messages.body_plain:
Hello, very interesting behaviour :)
I think it goes more into the root of the distributions used. Using Poisson regression may bring more information to the model and and a more precise posterior distribution will be obtain.
when you convert the data from count to 0/1 somehow you are loosing information, thus the estimates are more imprecise.

I quickly generated several data sets where the outcome is a Poisson distributed and the mean parameter is modeled via a random covariate. Build two GLM models (Poisson and Bernoulli distributed). Poisson model uses data as generated, for the Bernoulli model transform data to 0/1 is used, and run some MCMC. Standard deviation of the posterior distributions for the estimate value of the covariate are smaller in when the data used is count.

messages.subject: Re: N-micture model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Wenshuang,

I couldn't open your Zip, so I will try to answer and ask back from what I grasp from your text:
can you tell us how many cameras you have in all ? Is it just a single one ?
The standard binomial Nmix model of Royle 2004 only allows false negative errors, but NOT false positives. With camera traps usually you don't know how many photographs you make of the same individual (unless you can individually identify them, like for tigers with their stripes), so it is likely that you will count the same individual twice. That means, you double count, and that is a false-positive which is not allowed in this model. So, unless you somehow think you can exclude this possibility, I don't think the binomial Nmix model is adequate for your problem
There is a sister model, which is the Poisson-Poisson Nmixture model, which you can fit to the number of detections, regardless of the number of (repeat) detections per individual and occasion. In this sense, this model does allow for false positives and actually in the observation model estimates a detection rate (numbee of detections per individual). However, I think that this model can be very un-robust to violations of its parametric assumptions (the two Poissons). I have seen cases where it has yielded estimates of abundance that were quite unrealistic. But you may try it out and see what it gives.
Then, one fundamental limitation of any kind of these Nmixture models is that they are NOT areal-specific. That is, strictly you don't know the area to which your estimates "belong". So, the scaling up from the small areas sampled by the camtraps to the wider, large area is difficult or impossible.
Comments from anybody with more experience with camtraps most welcome !

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Using residuals from one part of a hierarchical model in another
messages.subject_clean: Using residuals from one part of a hierarchical model in another
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am trying to put together a hierarchical model with two parts - the first is a von Bertalanffy growth model <https://derekogle.com/NCNRS349/modules/PREP/NOTES/Growth> run in jags. People sometimes use the residuals from the von Bertalanffy curve as an index of growth rate, but the model to make the curve/index is run separately from the model used to find out what is explaining variation in the index.

Because this information all comes from one data set, I am hoping to be able to combine those steps, and use the residuals of the first part as a response in the second part of the model.

The first part should be (I think) like this:

size ~ dnorm(mu, tau)
mu <- von Bertalanffy equation
residual <- size-mu

Right now, because it can't define residual twice, I have the second part of the model as:

X ~ dnorm(mu1, tau1)
mu1 <- beta*residual + alpha

X represents a variable that might have a relationship with residual. That runs, but I don't think that is doing what we want, and it should be more like:

residual ~ dnorm(mu1,tau1)
mu1 <- beta*X + alpha

The objective is to find out whether X is explaining variation in residual, using residual as an index of growth rate.

So,  my two questions are (1) is calculating and using residuals this way appropriate/allowed in a Bayesian hierarchical model? And (2) if that is ok to do, is it possible to define the residuals in a way that would allow them to be used as a response rather than a predictor while keeping it in the same model as X, instead of two different models?

I'd super appreciate any thoughts folks have. Thank you for taking the time to read this!

Sarah

messages.subject: Re: N-micture model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Wenshuang,

the state model of an N-mixture model in algebra looks like this:

N_i ~ Poisson(lambda_i)

N_i is the realized abundance at site i, and lambda_i is the expected abundance at that site. Without a covariate in the model, lambda will be identical for all sites, but N_i will still be different. You can obtain estimates of N_i using function ranef().

To obtain a (perhaps) better characterization of spatial variability in abundance, you could add covariates into the model for lambda, thus doing something like this:

log(lambda_i) = alpha + beta1 * cov1_i + beta2 * cov2_i ....

If these covariates contain information about spatial variation in abundance, then (1) lambda_i will differ among sites and then represent an adequate measure of site-specific abundance, and (2) presumably the estimates of N_i obtained via ranef() will become better still.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Bad fit in removal sampling model?
messages.subject_clean: Bad fit in removal sampling model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm working on models examining avian point-count data using removal sampling in a Bayesian framework. The model is a three-part hierarchical model that estimates single-species detection, abundance, and availability separately. My main question is concerned with understanding covariates on the availability part of the model (things that are changing between visits to a site).

To examine model fit, I'm calculating a Bayesian p-value for each part of the model separately. I'm running into a lot of trouble getting usable Bayesian p-values for the availability part of my model (almost every time p-value = 0. A good p-value is around 0.5), and I'm wondering if this is because of lack of fit, or if I'm perhaps using the incorrect statistical test in the p-value calculation, or potentially some other reason. Currently, all three Bayesian p-values are calculated using a Freeman-Tukey test statistic.

Additionally, my mean detection probabilities are almost always quite low in these models (<10%). This is surprising because I have modeled these same data using N-mixture models and get reasonable detection probabilities (>20%). Is the availability structure of the model somehow pulling down my mean detection probability?

This problem occurs across all species tested (~20). All species are relatively common and abundant at our sites. All analyses use about 5 years of data, with >150 sites surveyed per year. All this is to say, this is not a data sparsity problem.

I have worked through a simulation of this model, and as far as I can tell, the code is correct. I've included a null version of the model (no covariates on any part of the model) in the attached R file, and have attached data from Green-tailed Towhees in 2018, a very common bird at our sites.

Running these data through the code in the R file gives these outputs (at 10,000 iterations, 3 chains):
Mean Detection: 0.137
Mean Availability: 0.81
Mean Abundance: 0.71
P-value Detection: 0.18
P-value Availability: 0
P-value Abundance: 0

Inclusion of covariates and random effects improves the abundance p-value. For example, when I run the full model with both fixed and random effects I get a Bayesian p-value for the abundance part of the model as 0.14. The availability p-value remains at 0. Mean detection decreases to 0.08.

Any insight on the issues I have highlighted above would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks for your time,
Martha

--
Martha Zillig, Ph.D.
(she/her)

Postdoctoral Fellow
Wildlife Biology Department
University of Montana
Stone Hall 112

website: marthazillig.github.io <http://marthazillig.github.io>

Dear Matt,

is this a static (a.k.a., single-season) occupancy model ? In that case, a random effect on occupancy is not identifiable. No replication there to estimate anything, only in detection.

Best regards  -- Marc

Subject: Random site effect on occupancy blowing up

Hi all,

I was demonstrating occupancy models in nimble for a colleague and simulated an occupancy model with one site covariate on occupancy and one site-by-survey covariate on detection. Then I added a random site effect to occupancy for demonstration and I noticed that the SD of the random effect was getting overestimated. I added more sites and surveys (went from 50/5 to 200/15) and the problem just seemed to get worse (see attached plot).

I'm wondering if I just misspecified something but I can't see what it would be. Could someone else take a look? Or is this a known issue with occupancy models?

Cheers,

Matt

在2023年5月14日星期日 UTC+8 14:31:04<marc.kery> 写道：
> Dear Wenshuang,
>
> the state model of an N-mixture model in algebra looks like this:
>
> N_i ~ Poisson(lambda_i)
>
> N_i is the realized abundance at site i, and lambda_i is the expected abundance at that site. Without a covariate in the model, lambda will be identical for all sites, but N_i will still be different. You can obtain estimates of N_i using function ranef().
>
> To obtain a (perhaps) better characterization of spatial variability in abundance, you could add covariates into the model for lambda, thus doing something like this:
>
> log(lambda_i) = alpha + beta1 * cov1_i + beta2 * cov2_i ....
>
> If these covariates contain information about spatial variation in abundance, then (1) lambda_i will differ among sites and then represent an adequate measure of site-specific abundance, and (2) presumably the estimates of N_i obtained via ranef() will become better still.
>
> Best regards  -- Marc
>
>
> From: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of wenshuang bao <bwens...@gmail.com>
> Sent: Sunday, May 14, 2023 04:39
>
> To: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: N-micture model
>
> Dear Marc,
>
> Thanks for your help sincerely! I have read your response carefully.
>
> There are 60 infrared cameras in our study area. I want to use the mixture model to calculate the relative abundance of animals at each camera point, but the code I sent you turns out to be an average relative abundance for the entire area, which is different from the relative abundance I needed for each camera point. I don't know if my needs can be realized, which is distubing.
>
> I have changed the format of the attachment. I wonder if you can download it this time. Sincerely thank you for helping me check again.
>
> 在2023年5月12日星期五 UTC+8 01:51:25<marc.kery> 写道：
> > Dear Wenshuang,
> >
> > I couldn't open your Zip, so I will try to answer and ask back from what I grasp from your text:
> > can you tell us how many cameras you have in all ? Is it just a single one ?
> > The standard binomial Nmix model of Royle 2004 only allows false negative errors, but NOT false positives. With camera traps usually you don't know how many photographs you make of the same individual (unless you can individually identify them, like for tigers with their stripes), so it is likely that you will count the same individual twice. That means, you double count, and that is a false-positive which is not allowed in this model. So, unless you somehow think you can exclude this possibility, I don't think the binomial Nmix model is adequate for your problem
> > There is a sister model, which is the Poisson-Poisson Nmixture model, which you can fit to the number of detections, regardless of the number of (repeat) detections per individual and occasion. In this sense, this model does allow for false positives and actually in the observation model estimates a detection rate (numbee of detections per individual). However, I think that this model can be very un-robust to violations of its parametric assumptions (the two Poissons). I have seen cases where it has yielded estimates of abundance that were quite unrealistic. But you may try it out and see what it gives.
> > Then, one fundamental limitation of any kind of these Nmixture models is that they are NOT areal-specific. That is, strictly you don't know the area to which your estimates "belong". So, the scaling up from the small areas sampled by the camtraps to the wider, large area is difficult or impossible.
> > Comments from anybody with more experience with camtraps most welcome !
> >
> > Best regards  --- Marc
> >
> >

I have tried the code about N-mixture model and have some questions.
> > Whether the final result of the model is the relative abundance of the selected animals in the whole area, if so, the gradient prediction of relative abundance cannot be performed. Can I calculate the  relative abundance of animals at a single camera site using data from only one camera site?
> >
> > The attachment contains my code and data. I sincerely request you to help me guide.

messages.subject: integrating telemetry and CMR data
messages.body_plain:
Maybe a crazy idea but I have been looking in the literature to see if anyone has tried to integrate telemetry and spatially explicit CMR (SCR) data in an open population context.  I have not found much.  I am not talking about using telemetry to estimate the scaling parameter (sigma) for the detection function, but using survival rate (S) and recruitment estimates from telemetry to help with the estimation of phi and f in a Jolly Seber-type model.  I realize that phi includes emigration and S does not, but there are dispersal data embedded in the SCR data too are there not?  Per capita recruitment from telemetry and apparent recruitment (f) from SCR should be similarly (but in reverse) related.  I have long-term CMR and telemetry data on a bear population and it seems a shame not to integrate them in a unified approach for estimating population dynamics.  Thanks for any thoughts.
Joe

messages.subject: Node inconsistent with parent in Poisson observation model of count data
messages.subject_clean: Node inconsistent with parent in Poisson observation model of count data
messages.body_plain:
Hello every, I am hoping I might get some advice on what I suspect to be a rather silly question. I am running an IPM and using a state-space model to analyze the count data. For the observation model I am using a Poisson distribution, which works wonderfully when using deterministic process equations. But when I add in demographic stochasticity I keep getting the "Node inconsistent with parents" error referring to the count data (in the examle below, the specific error is "3 nodes produced errors; first error: Error in node C[21] Node inconsistent with parents")

Population model code:

# Population count data (state-space model)
# Model for the initial stage-specific population sizes

N1  ~ dnorm(2000,0.01)I(0,)
N[1,1] <- round(N1)
N2  ~ dnorm(2000,0.01)I(0,)
N[2,1] <- round(N2)
N3  ~ dnorm(2000,0.01)I(0,)
N[3,1] <- round(N3)
N4 ~ dnorm(8000,0.01)I(0,)
N[4,1] <- round(N4)

# Process model over time: our model of population dynamics
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
  N[1,t+1] ~ dpois(N[4,t] * fecund[t] / 2 * alpha[1,t])
  N[2,t+1] ~ dbin(alpha[1,t], N[1,t])
  N[3,t+1] ~ dbin(alpha[1,t], N[2,t])
  N[4,t+1] ~ dbin(alpha[2,t], N[3,t]+N[4,t])
}

# Observation model
for (t in 1:n.occasions){
  C[t] ~ dpois(N[4,t])
}

Where C[t] = c(NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,8024,NA,NA,7334,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,7729,NA,NA,NA,6374,4796,NA,NA,8635)
.
Again, I apologize for what is likely a silly question. Ideally I would use a normal distribution to define my observation equation but my observed and estimated counts are quite different when I don't use the Poisson. Any advice or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarah,
The strategy I would suggest to debug this would be to create a model with nimbleModel, calculate, and look at individual nodes. For example, if model is the result of nimbleModel, you could look at:
model$calculate() # probably -Inf or NaN if something is not valid
model$calculate("C[21]")  # confirm a problem specifically for C[21]
model$C[21] # look at the value
model$N[4, 21] # Look at the value: is it valid as a Poisson parameter given the value of c[21]?
etc.
Given the temporal sequence of dbin, a first guess would be if N[4, 21] is 0 and C[21] is not 0.
If you are not providing inits for all of the N[,] values, then many of them might simply be NA. If you need values filled in, you could use model$simulate('N')
HTH. If you're still stuck, please see if you can send a fully reproducible example.
Perry
